title: Joshua 9:16–27
context: Three days later Israel learns that the Gibeonites are neighbors, living in four nearby cities. The congregation grumbles, but the princes refuse to break an oath sworn by the LORD, the God of Israel. Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who explain that fear of the LORD’s command drove them to the deception. They are spared and made wood cutters and water drawers for the congregation and the LORD’s altar. Later texts show the oath still binding Israel generations afterward (2 Samuel 21:1–14).

verses.text: At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors, and that they lived among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Within three days Israel learns that the Gibeonites are neighbors. Arminian readers note how quickly the deception unravels, leaving Israel bound by a promise it would not have made had it known the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the discovery as exposing the leaders’ failure to inquire of God (9:14). Shared ground: the short interval highlights how avoidable the mistake was, and how the consequences of a hasty oath cannot simply be undone.

verses.text: The children of Israel traveled and came to their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel reaches Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim. Arminian readers note that Gibeon headed a small league of towns; Gibeon itself is commonly placed north of Jerusalem, though other site identifications are less certain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Kiriath Jearim later houses the ark for a time (1 Samuel 7:1–2), so the spared towns go on to play a part in Israel’s worship. Both traditions read the list as showing that the treaty covered a group of cities.

verses.text: The children of Israel didn’t strike them, because the princes of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. All the congregation murmured against the princes.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel does not strike them because the princes swore by the LORD, and the congregation murmurs. Arminian readers see a tension between popular frustration and the leaders’ sense that an oath in God’s name must be honored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the name of the LORD makes the oath sacred, so breaking it would profane His name. Shared ground: both traditions read the princes’ restraint as right, and the people’s grumbling as understandable but mistaken.

verses.text: But all the princes said to all the congregation, “We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Now therefore we may not touch them.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes refuse to touch the Gibeonites because they swore by the God of Israel. Arminian readers see integrity under pressure: an oath remains binding even when the other side lied to obtain it, as Psalm 15:4 commends keeping one’s word when it hurts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold that oaths before God bind the conscience, and that God’s honor is bound up with Israel’s faithfulness to its word. Both traditions treat this verse as a clear example of oath-keeping as a covenant duty.

verses.text: We will do this to them, and let them live; lest wrath be on us, because of the oath which we swore to them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The princes fear wrath if they break the oath. Arminian readers note that this fear proves well-founded: when Saul later attacks the Gibeonites, a famine follows and the wrong must be addressed (2 Samuel 21:1–14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the later famine God’s own confirmation that the oath was binding on Israel across generations. Shared ground: the princes rightly judge that violating a sworn covenant would bring divine displeasure on the nation.

verses.text: The princes said to them, “Let them live.” So they became wood cutters and drawers of water for all the congregation, as the princes had spoken to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites live but become wood cutters and drawers of water. Arminian readers see a compromise that keeps the oath while placing the deceivers in a subordinate role, similar to the low-status labor named in Deuteronomy 29:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the role keeps the Gibeonites alive within Israel and bound to serve, fulfilling their own claim to be servants. Both traditions read the arrangement as both mercy and consequence for the deception.

verses.text: Joshua called for them, and he spoke to them, saying, “Why have you deceived us, saying, ‘We are very far from you,’ when you live among us?
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua confronts the Gibeonites directly about their lie. Arminian readers note that he names the wrong plainly, making clear that keeping the oath does not mean approving the means by which it was obtained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Joshua’s rebuke as upholding truthfulness even while honoring the covenant. Shared ground: the narrative keeps two things together, that the Gibeonites deceived Israel and that Israel must still keep its word.

verses.text: Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you will never fail to be slaves, both wood cutters and drawers of water for the house of my God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua declares them cursed, bound to serve as wood cutters and water drawers for the house of God. Arminian readers note the irony that people under judgment are brought into service connected with Israel’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God turning a curse into a place near His sanctuary, a picture of grace working through judgment. Both traditions note that the curse here takes the form of permanent service, not death, which the oath had ruled out.

verses.text: They answered Joshua, and said, “Because your servants were certainly told how the LORD your God commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land, and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you. Therefore we were very afraid for our lives because of you, and have done this thing.
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites admit they acted out of fear because they knew of the LORD’s command through Moses. Arminian readers see a people who believed God’s word about the land and acted to save their lives, even by wrong means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Gibeonites understood the command to destroy the inhabitants (Deuteronomy 7:1–2) and took it seriously. Shared ground: their fear reflects belief that the LORD’s word would be carried out.

verses.text: Now, behold, we are in your hand. Do to us as it seems good and right to you to do.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites place themselves in Joshua’s hands, asking him to do what seems good and right. Arminian readers see a full surrender, a contrast with the kings who chose to fight rather than to submit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that their surrender leads to preservation, an echo of Rahab’s request for mercy (2:12–13). Both traditions read the verse as a turn from deception to open submission before Israel’s leader.

verses.text: He did so to them, and delivered them out of the hand of the children of Israel, so that they didn’t kill them.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua delivers them from the people, who might otherwise have killed them. Arminian readers credit Joshua with protecting the Gibeonites and restraining the anger of the congregation in order to keep Israel’s oath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Joshua acting as a faithful covenant leader who guards Israel from breaking its word. Shared ground: Joshua’s intervention shows that leadership in Israel included protecting those to whom the nation had bound itself.

verses.text: That day Joshua made them wood cutters and drawers of water for the congregation and for the LORD’s altar to this day, in the place which he should choose.
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites serve the congregation and the LORD’s altar in the place He would choose. Arminian readers note the link to Deuteronomy 12:5 and see the outsiders included, though in a lowly role, in Israel’s worshiping life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that men of Gibeon are later named among those who helped rebuild Jerusalem’s wall (Nehemiah 3:7), a sign of lasting inclusion. Both traditions read the phrase “to this day” as the narrator’s note that the arrangement endured.
